title: Fractions: Recurring Decimals, Mixed Numbers and Order of Operations
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Mathematics 0862 · Stage 8 · Number
summary: Recognise recurring decimals, subtract mixed numbers, multiply a whole number by a mixed number, divide a whole number by a fraction, and use the laws of arithmetic with fractions and decimals.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Recognise fractions that are equal to recurring decimals, for example 1/3 = 0.333… and 2/11 = 0.1818… (8Nf.01)
Estimate and subtract mixed numbers, and write the answer as a mixed number in its simplest form (8Nf.02)
Estimate and multiply a whole number by a mixed number, and divide a whole number by a proper fraction (8Nf.03)
Use the laws of arithmetic and the order of operations (including brackets) to simplify calculations with decimals or fractions (8Nf.04)

blocks.text: This page has four parts: (1) fractions that turn into **recurring decimals**, (2) **subtracting mixed numbers**, (3) **multiplying** a whole number by a mixed number and **dividing** a whole number by a fraction, and (4) using the **laws of arithmetic** to make fraction and decimal calculations easier. All of this can appear on the non-calculator paper, so the methods are written out by hand.
Key words

items: terminating decimal
عشري منتهي — a decimal that stops: 3/8 = 0.375
recurring decimal
عشري دوري (متكرر) — a decimal where a digit or a block of digits repeats for ever: 1/3 = 0.333…
mixed number
عدد كسري — a whole number and a proper fraction: 2 7/12
improper fraction
كسر غير حقيقي — numerator bigger than denominator: 31/12
simplest form
أبسط صورة — numerator and denominator have no common factor except 1
reciprocal
المقلوب — the fraction turned upside down: the reciprocal of 3/4 is 4/3
commutative law
خاصية الإبدال — order does not matter for + and ×: 0.25 × 7 = 7 × 0.25
associative law
خاصية الدمج (التجميع) — grouping does not matter for + and ×: (0.25 × 4) × 7.3 = 0.25 × (4 × 7.3)
distributive law
خاصية التوزيع — a × b + a × c = a × (b + c)

blocks.text: 1. Fractions and recurring decimals

A fraction is a division: 3/8 means 3 ÷ 8. Doing the division gives the decimal. Sometimes the division **stops** (a terminating decimal); sometimes it **never stops** because the same remainders come round again and again (a recurring decimal).

rows: remainder 1 every time, so the digit 3 repeats
8, then remainder 2 every time, so 3 repeats

blocks.text: **Dot notation.** Instead of writing "…", mathematicians put a **dot over** the digit that repeats. If a **block** of digits repeats, put a dot over the **first and last** digit of the block.

rows: one digit, then the repeat starts
a block of six digits repeats

blocks.text: **Calculators round the last digit.** A calculator may show 2/3 as 0.6666666667. That 7 is only the calculator rounding — 2/3 = 0.666… recurring. Do not say "it terminates" just because the screen is full.
2. Subtracting mixed numbers
**Always estimate first.** Round each mixed number to the nearest whole number (or half). For 5 1/4 − 2 2/3: about 5 − 3 = 2, and a bit more because 2 2/3 was rounded up. So expect a little over 2.
**Method A — change to improper fractions** (safe and always works):

items: Write each mixed number as an improper fraction: 5 1/4 = 21/4 and 2 2/3 = 8/3.
Use a common denominator (the LCM of 4 and 3 is 12): 21/4 = 63/12 and 8/3 = 32/12.
Subtract the numerators: 63/12 − 32/12 = 31/12.
Change back to a mixed number and simplify: 31 ÷ 12 = 2 remainder 7, so **2 7/12**. (7 and 12 have no common factor.) This matches the estimate.

blocks.text: **Method B — wholes and fractions separately** (quicker with small numbers, but watch the fractions):

items: Common denominator: 5 1/4 − 2 2/3 = 5 3/12 − 2 8/12.
3/12 is smaller than 8/12, so you cannot take 8/12 away. **Exchange** one whole for 12/12: 5 3/12 = 4 15/12.

blocks.text: **Simplest form.** The answer must be a mixed number with the fraction part in its simplest form: 3 6/8 should be written 3 3/4, and 2 15/12 is not finished — it is 3 3/12 = 3 1/4.
3. Multiplying a whole number by a mixed number
**Estimate:** 4 × 2 3/5 is between 4 × 2 = 8 and 4 × 3 = 12. As 2 3/5 is a bit more than 2 1/2, the answer is a bit more than 4 × 2 1/2 = 10.
**Method 1 — split the mixed number** (this is the distributive law):

blocks.text: **Method 2 — improper fraction:** 2 3/5 = 13/5, so 4 × 13/5 = 52/5 = 52 ÷ 5 = 10 remainder 2 = **10 2/5**. Both methods agree, and the answer is close to the estimate 10.
4. Dividing a whole number by a proper fraction
6 ÷ 3/4 asks: **how many 3/4 fit into 6?** Draw it: 6 wholes are 24 quarters, and 24 quarters make 8 groups of 3 quarters.

blocks.text: **The quick method: multiply by the reciprocal.** Dividing by 3/4 is the same as multiplying by 4/3 ("keep, change, flip": keep the 6, change ÷ to ×, flip 3/4 to 4/3).

items: = **8** ✓ (the same as the diagram)

blocks.text: **Sense check:** dividing by a fraction less than 1 gives an answer **bigger** than the number you started with. 3/4 fits into 1 more than once, so it fits into 6 more than 6 times.

blocks.title: افتكر القاعدة دي
items: طرح الأعداد الكسرية: قدّر الأول، وبعدين حوّل لكسور غير حقيقية بمقام مشترك، واطرح، وارجع لعدد كسري في أبسط صورة.
القسمة على كسر = الضرب في مقلوبه: ٦ ÷ ٣/٤ = ٦ × ٤/٣ = ٨. والناتج بيكبر لأننا بنقسم على حاجة أصغر من ١.
الكسر العشري الدوري: رقم أو مجموعة أرقام بتتكرر للأبد، زي ١/٣ = ٠٫٣٣٣…

blocks.text: 5. Laws of arithmetic and order of operations with decimals and fractions

The order of operations is the same as for whole numbers: **Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication (left to right), Addition and Subtraction (left to right)**. The laws of arithmetic let you **reorder** or **regroup** to make a calculation easy without a calculator.
**Brackets change the answer:**
**Subtraction and division are not commutative:** 5 − 2 1/2 ≠ 2 1/2 − 5, and 6 ÷ 3/4 ≠ 3/4 ÷ 6. Only swap the order for + and ×.
Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — (a) Write 7/9 as a decimal. (b) Draw a ring around the fraction that is equal to a recurring decimal: 2/5 5/6 7/20 3/8 [2 marks]

items: (a) Ninths: the numerator repeats, so 7/9 = **0.777…** (written 0.7 with a dot over the 7). Check: 7 ÷ 9 = 0 r 7, 70 ÷ 9 = 7 r 7, 70 ÷ 9 = 7 r 7 … the remainder 7 keeps coming back.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — Work out 4 3/8 − 1 5/6. Give your answer as a mixed number in its simplest form. [2 marks]

items: Estimate: about 4 1/2 − 2 = 2 1/2.
Improper fractions: 4 3/8 = 35/8 and 1 5/6 = 11/6.
Common denominator 24: 35/8 = 105/24 and 11/6 = 44/24. (1 mark for a correct common denominator.)
105/24 − 44/24 = 61/24 = 2 remainder 13 → **2 13/24**. (13 is prime and does not divide 24, so this is the simplest form.) Close to the estimate ✓

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** subtracting the fractions the wrong way round: 4 − 1 = 3 and 5/6 − 3/8 = 11/24, giving 3 11/24. You cannot take 20/24 from 9/24 without exchanging a whole.
**Worked example 3** — Work out 3 × 4 5/6. Give your answer as a mixed number in its simplest form. [2 marks]

Estimate: 3 × 5 = 15, a bit less. Split: 3 × 4 = 12 and 3 × 5/6 = 15/6 = 2 3/6 = 2 1/2. Add: 12 + 2 1/2 = **14 1/2** ✓. **Common mistake:** multiplying only the whole number (3 × 4 5/6 = 12 5/6) — the fraction part must be multiplied too.
**Worked example 4** — A ribbon is 9 m long. It is cut into pieces that are each 3/5 m long. How many pieces are there? [2 marks]

items: "How many 3/5 fit into 9?" → 9 ÷ 3/5.
Check: 15 × 3/5 = 45/5 = 9 ✓. The answer is more than 9 because each piece is shorter than 1 m.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — Without a calculator, work out 4.6 × 0.7 + 5.4 × 0.7. Show how you used a law of arithmetic. [2 marks]
Both terms have the factor 0.7, so use the distributive law: (4.6 + 5.4) × 0.7 = 10 × 0.7 = **7**. Much quicker than working out 3.22 + 3.78.
**Worked example 6** — Work out 2/3 + 1/3 × (5/2 − 1). [2 marks]
**Common mistake:** adding first (2/3 + 1/3 = 1, then 1 × 3/2 = 3/2). Multiplication comes before addition.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Thinking a decimal terminates because the calculator screen is full: 2/3 shows as 0.6666666667, but it recurs.
Putting the dots on the wrong digits: 0.1818… has dots over the 1 and the 8 (the first and last digits of the repeating block).
Subtracting mixed numbers without a common denominator, or taking the smaller fraction from the bigger one when it is the wrong way round.
Leaving an answer like 2 14/12 or 3 6/8 — change to a proper mixed number in its simplest form.
Multiplying only the whole part: 4 × 2 3/5 is not 8 3/5.
Flipping the wrong fraction when dividing: 6 ÷ 3/4 = 6 × 4/3, not 1/6 × 3/4.
Working left to right when × or ÷ comes after + or −. Brackets first, then × and ÷, then + and −.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Draw a ring around the fraction that is equal to a recurring decimal" or "Tick the fractions that are recurring decimals".

"Work out 5 1/4 − 2 2/3. Give your answer as a mixed number in its simplest form." — usually 2 marks: 1 for a correct method (e.g. a correct common denominator), 1 for the final answer. An answer that is not in simplest form can lose the final mark.
"Estimate …" — show the rounded numbers. An exact answer with no estimate may get no mark.
Word problems with division by a fraction: "How many 3/4-litre glasses can be filled from 6 litres?" — write the division first.
"Use the distributive law to work out …" or "Show how you can work out … without a calculator" — show the regrouped calculation, not just the answer.
Spot the mistake in a student's working, then correct it (Thinking and Working Mathematically: critiquing).

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Fractions — practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, from easy to Checkpoint-hard. No calculator. Type fractions like 7/12 and mixed numbers like 2 3/4 (whole number, space, fraction). For the explain question, mark yourself with the mark scheme.

questions.q: Which fraction is equal to a recurring decimal?
Which is the best estimate for 8 1/9 − 3 6/7?
Work out 7 1/3 − 2 3/4. Give your answer as a mixed number in its simplest form.

questions.p: A bottle holds 5 1/2 litres of water. Amira pours out 2 3/4 litres.
questions.q: How much water is left in the bottle?
Work out 6 × 2 3/4. Give your answer as a mixed number in its simplest form.

questions.p: A jug holds 3 litres of juice. Each glass holds 3/7 of a litre.
questions.q: How many glasses can be filled from the jug?
Work out 7 ÷ 4/5. Give your answer as a mixed number.
questions.e: 7 × 5/4 = 35/4 (1 mark). 35 ÷ 4 = 8 remainder 3, so 8 3/4. The answer is bigger than 7 because 4/5 is less than 1 ✓.

questions.q: Use the laws of arithmetic to work out 2.7 × 3.8 + 2.7 × 6.2
Work out 3/4 − 1/2 × 1/3. Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.e: Multiply first: 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6 (1 mark). Then 3/4 − 1/6 = 9/12 − 2/12 = 7/12. (Working left to right gives (3/4 − 1/2) × 1/3 = 1/12, which is wrong.)

questions.q: Karim works out 4 1/5 − 1 3/5. He writes: 4 − 1 = 3 and 3/5 − 1/5 = 2/5, so the answer is 3 2/5. Explain his mistake and work out the correct answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: explains that he took 1/5 from 3/5 (the wrong way round); he should take 3/5 from 1/5, which needs exchanging a whole (accept: he should have changed to improper fractions). 1 mark: correct answer 2 3/5 (accept 13/5). Do not accept a mistake description such as "he forgot a common denominator" (the denominators are already the same).
questions.e: The calculation is 1/5 − 3/5, not 3/5 − 1/5. Because 1/5 is smaller than 3/5, exchange a whole: 4 1/5 = 3 6/5. Then 3 6/5 − 1 3/5 = 2 3/5. Check with improper fractions: 21/5 − 8/5 = 13/5 = 2 3/5.

blocks.title: Remember
items: A fraction is a division. If the division never stops, the decimal recurs: 1/3 = 0.333…, 2/11 = 0.1818…, 1/6 = 0.1666…
Subtracting mixed numbers: estimate, use a common denominator, exchange a whole if needed (or use improper fractions), and give the answer as a mixed number in simplest form.
Whole number × mixed number: multiply the whole part and the fraction part, then add. 4 × 2 3/5 = 8 + 2 2/5 = 10 2/5.
Whole number ÷ fraction: multiply by the reciprocal. 6 ÷ 3/4 = 6 × 4/3 = 8 — bigger than 6.
Brackets, then × and ÷, then + and −. Use the commutative, associative and distributive laws to make calculations easier.
